posts.title: The 5 Numbers Every Investor Must Know
posts.excerpt: Before you buy a single share or property, learn these five numbers — they will save you from the most expensive mistakes in finance.

content.heading: Number 1: Your compounding rate
paragraphs: Every financial decision is a compounding decision. The Rule of 72 — divide 72 by your annual return to get your doubling time — turns any rate into a timeline. At 8% your money doubles every 9 years; at 12% every 6 years. That four-point difference is the difference between retiring rich and retiring comfortable.
The number matters because it forces you to see fees for what they are: a compounding tax that quietly steals a third of your lifetime returns.

content.heading: Number 2: Cash-on-cash return
paragraphs: Rental property returns are quoted in many ways, but the one that matters for your wallet is cash-on-cash: annual cash flow divided by the cash you actually put in. A deal that returns 10% cash-on-cash before appreciation beats a 'big' deal that ties up your capital for 4%.
Underwrite every real estate deal with this number and you'll stop overpaying for the illusion of appreciation.

content.heading: Number 3: Net worth, not income
paragraphs: Track your net worth monthly — assets minus liabilities. Income is a river; net worth is the reservoir. Two people earning the same salary can have a 10x difference in net worth simply by how they allocate what flows through their hands.
The moment you start measuring the reservoir instead of the river, your decisions change.

content.heading: Numbers 4 & 5: Savings rate and the 4% rule
paragraphs: Your savings rate — the percentage of income you keep — is the single most controllable lever of your wealth timeline. Bump it from 10% to 20% and you can cut years off your journey.

And once assets outnumber expenses, the 4% rule tells you how much you can safely withdraw: multiply your annual spending by 25 — that's your FIRE number. It converts an abstract dream into a concrete target.

posts.title: How We Priced Our First SaaS and Doubled Profit
posts.excerpt: The highest-leverage decision we ever made wasn't a feature — it was a price change. Here's the exact framework we used.

content.heading: The mistake we all make
paragraphs: We launched our first SaaS at $9/month because it felt safe. Ninety days later we had users but no business — our customer acquisition cost was eating the entire lifetime value.
The fix wasn't more marketing. It was price. We moved to a three-tier structure and raised the middle tier 40%.

content.heading: The three-tier framework
paragraphs: Tier one is your entry offer: cheap, simple, and designed to get people through the door. Tier two is your real product — the one you actually want to sell. Tier three exists to make tier two look reasonable.
Most revenue comes from the middle. The premium tier is an anchor, and a good anchor makes the middle feel like a bargain.

content.heading: The results
paragraphs: Revenue per customer doubled, support tickets dropped (higher-paying customers churn less), and our acquisition math finally worked. The same number of customers now produced nearly double the profit.
If you haven't changed your price in the last 12 months, you are almost certainly underpriced. Raise it 20% and watch what happens — the data will tell you the truth.

posts.title: AI Won't Replace You — But Someone Using AI Will
posts.excerpt: The biggest wealth transfer of our generation belongs to people who pair deep domain knowledge with AI leverage. Here's how to position yourself.

content.heading: The leverage is permissionless
paragraphs: Code and media are the permissionless levers of wealth — and AI just made both dramatically more powerful. A single person with a model API and domain knowledge can now ship what used to take a team of ten.
The people building fortunes aren't the ones asking whether AI will replace them. They're the ones asking which workflow they know intimately enough to automate.

content.heading: Domain knowledge is the moat
paragraphs: Models are commoditizing fast. What they can't commoditize is your judgment: which industry, which workflow, which customer, which objection. The vertical AI tools that win — in legal, healthcare, construction — are built by people who understood the domain first.
Pick one industry you know, find the most hated manual task in it, and automate it with an existing model API. That's the entire playbook.

content.heading: Your 90-day AI plan
paragraphs: Days 1-30: learn prompt engineering and API integration by building a toy project. Days 31-60: interview 20 practitioners about their most hated task. Days 61-90: ship a prototype to 10 of them and watch what they do with it.
The AI economy rewards builders, not spectators. Start this week.

posts.title: The Power of Losing: What Failure Taught Me
posts.excerpt: I made my first million at 27 and lost all of it at 28. Rebuilding taught me more than the winning ever did.

content.heading: The wipeout
paragraphs: At 27 I was up. At 28 I was flat broke, owing money to people I respected, and sitting in a borrowed apartment trying to figure out what happened. I had confused a good run with a good system.
The hardest part wasn't the money. It was the story I told myself about being smart — because that story had made me careless.

content.heading: The four lessons that rebuilt me
paragraphs: First: never risk what you can't afford to lose. Second: debrief every loss within 48 hours, in writing. Third: size every bet so that no single failure ends the game. Fourth: the market doesn't care how much you know — it pays for what you do.
I came back by 31, slower and richer. The system replaced the ego, and the system compounds.

content.heading: Why failure is tuition
paragraphs: Every billionaire in our curriculum has a wipeout story — Dalio, Jobs, Bezos's early missteps. The pattern isn't avoiding loss; it's industrializing recovery.
Build your tilt insurance now: a cash buffer, a peer group that normalizes loss, and a journal. When the bad bet comes — and it will — you'll pay the tuition once and keep the education.

posts.title: House Hacking 101: My First Property at 22
posts.excerpt: I bought my first four-plex with a 3.5% down payment, lived in one unit, and haven't paid rent since. Here's exactly how.

content.heading: Why house hacking is the best first deal
paragraphs: A multi-unit property you live in turns your biggest expense into an income stream. Three tenants pay the mortgage; you live free — or get paid to live. It's the cheapest, lowest-risk way to enter real estate, and the FHA loan only needs 3.5% down.
I bought my first four-plex at 22 with $12,000 down. My cost of housing went from $1,100/month in rent to zero — and I owned an asset that appreciated while my tenants paid it off.

content.heading: The deal math that matters
paragraphs: Underwrite with three numbers: the 1% rule (monthly rent should be roughly 1% of purchase price), cap rate, and cash-on-cash return. Then stress-test: what does the deal look like if one unit sits vacant for 60 days? If you can survive that, you can survive real estate.
Walk the property with the inspector, talk to the neighbors, and read the actual lease documents. Cheap diligence now prevents expensive surprises later.

content.heading: The path from one door to many
paragraphs: Once your house hack is stabilized, refinance to pull equity out, rent your unit, and repeat with the next property. That's the BRRRR machine — Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat.
Every real estate empire in our founder circle started with a single ugly first deal. Yours can too.

posts.title: Building a Personal Brand That Compounds
posts.excerpt: A personal brand is the highest-ROI asset you can build in 2026 — and it's permissionless. Here's the exact 90-day engine.

content.heading: Why your name is an asset
paragraphs: Trust is the scarcest currency in the economy, and a personal brand manufactures it at scale. When you're known as the person who teaches X brilliantly, deals find you: partnerships, board seats, advisory fees — without a single cold email.
Positioning beats popularity. Being the go-to for a specific niche is worth more than being vaguely known by everyone.

content.heading: The 90-day content engine
paragraphs: Choose one platform and one niche. Publish twice weekly for 90 days: one teach piece, one story piece, one reaction piece. Reply to every thoughtful comment. Track which format drives the most conversation and double down.
Consistency over intensity: one high-quality piece per week for three years beats a viral burst and silence. Compounding is the whole game.

content.heading: Monetize late, not early
paragraphs: Build the audience and the trust first. When you do offer something, make it the natural next step for people who already trust you — a course, a cohort, a service.
The students in our program who built brands first are the ones closing enterprise deals without a sales team. The brand is the funnel.
